step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: A 70-year-old male returned traveler from Senegal presenting with fever, liver abscesses, and bacteremia

step5_concept_grounding: Non-O1, non-O139 Vibrio cholerae bacteremia with hepatic abscesses; toxigenic cholera ruled out

evidence_items.source_quote: One of the two sets of blood cultures collected upon admission yielded a Gram-negative rod, compatible with V. cholerae (Fig. 2). Stool cultures were negative.
evidence_items.target_concept: Vibrio cholerae bacteremia with negative stool culture

evidence_items.source_quote: The strain did not agglutinate when tested against O1 or O139 antisera. PCR techniques demonstrated the absence of the major virulence-encoding genes of toxigenic V. cholerae, the cholera-toxin (ctxA and ctxB) and the toxin-coregulated pilus (tcpA) virulence genes, and of the stn gene, encoding a heat-stable enterotoxin reported to contribute to the pathogenicity of NOVC.
evidence_items.test_name: National Reference Center seroagglutination and virulence PCR
evidence_items.target_concept: O1/O139 agglutination and cholera toxin (ctxA, ctxB)

step10_contradiction_notes: Suspicion of cholera or toxigenic V. cholerae ruled out by negative stool culture, negative O1/O139 seroagglutination, and negative cholera toxin PCR (ctxA/ctxB).
rationale: A 70-year-old male returned from Senegal with watery diarrhea, fever, and liver abscesses. Blood culture grew Vibrio cholerae, but evaluation at the National Reference Center proved negative for O1 and O139 antisera, negative for cholera toxin genes (ctxA/ctxB), and stool cultures were negative. Cholera was definitively tested and ruled out, and the patient was diagnosed with non-O1/non-O139 pyogenic liver abscess and bacteremia. VPD not satisfied -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 61-year-old male presenting with acute pancreatitis and Aeromonas hydrophila sepsis following raw oyster consumption.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae infection tested and ruled out during microbiological workup

evidence_items.source_quote: Test for Vibrio cholera was negative.
Sequencing via rpoD gene confirmed A. hydrophila.

step10_contradiction_notes: Testing for Vibrio cholerae was explicitly negative, and rpoD gene sequencing confirmed Aeromonas hydrophila.
rationale: A 61-year-old male presented with acute pancreatitis and sepsis after consuming raw oysters in Florida. Blood cultures grew Gram-negative bacilli confirmed as Aeromonas hydrophila by MicroScan and rpoD gene sequencing, while testing for Vibrio cholerae was explicitly negative -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 8-year-old girl with epilepsy and HLA-B*15:02-positive carbamazepine-induced toxic epidermal necrolysis complicated by severe gastrointestinal involvement.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae tested and ruled out via 24-pathogen stool real-time PCR panel and stool culture

evidence_items.source_quote: However, a stool real-time PCR failed to detect 24 infectious pathogens, involving Vibrio vulnificus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, Vibrio cholera, Campylobacter spp. (C. jejuni, C. upsaliensis, and C. coli), Salmonella spp., Clostridium difficile (tcdA/tcdB), Yersinia enterocolitica, EAEC, ETEC, STEC, STEC O157:H7, EPEC, EIEC, Plesiomonasshigelloides, Norovirus GI and GII, Rotavirus A, Astrovirus, Spovirus GI, GII, GIV, GV, Entamoebahistolytica, Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia lamblia, and Cyclosporacayetanensis.

evidence_items.target_concept: Enteric bacterial pathogens including Vibrio cholerae

step10_contradiction_notes: Stool real-time PCR for 24 enteric pathogens (explicitly including Vibrio cholerae) and stool cultures were negative.
rationale: An 8-year-old girl with carbamazepine-induced toxic epidermal necrolysis developed severe watery bloody diarrhea (15-20 stools/day) on hospital day 3. Stool real-time PCR failed to detect 24 enteric pathogens including Vibrio cholerae, and stool cultures were also negative, confirming TEN-related gastrointestinal mucosal involvement rather than cholera -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 50-year-old female returning traveler from Lagos, Nigeria diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria and Salmonella enterica serovar Stanleyville bacteremia.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio and Vibrio cholerae tested negative by BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel NAAT on stool

evidence_items.source_quote: Nucleic acid amplification-based testing of a stool specimen was negative for adenovirus, Campylobacter, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Clostridium difficile, enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, enteropathogenic E. coli, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shiga-like toxin producing E. coli, Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, human astrovirus, norovirus GI/GII, Plesiomonas shigelloides, rotavirus A, Salmonella, sapovirus, Vibrio, Vibrio cholera, and Yersinia enterocolitica (FilmArray  Gastrointestinal Panel, BioFire Diagnostics LLC, Salt Lake City, UT).

step10_contradiction_notes: Stool nucleic acid amplification panel was explicitly negative for Vibrio and Vibrio cholerae.
rationale: A 50-year-old female returning from Nigeria presented with diarrhea, fevers, and syncope, and was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria and nontyphoidal Salmonella enterica serovar Stanleyville bacteremia. Stool nucleic acid amplification testing (BioFire FilmArray Gastrointestinal Panel) was explicitly negative for Vibrio and Vibrio cholerae -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 57-year-old HIV-positive Indian male presenting with 4 months of large-volume watery diarrhea diagnosed as eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae tested negative on stool analysis and culture

evidence_items.source_quote: Stool analysis including culture was negative for Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, Vibrio cholerae, acid-fast bacteria, or any other parasites.

step10_contradiction_notes: Stool analysis including culture was negative for Vibrio cholerae; duodenal biopsy confirmed eosinophilic gastroenteritis.
rationale: A 57-year-old male with HIV presented with 4 months of large-volume watery diarrhea and 20 kg weight loss. Stool analysis including culture was explicitly negative for Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, and acid-fast bacteria, and upper gastrointestinal biopsies established eosinophilic gastroenteritis -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 74-year-old male presenting with bloody diarrhea and fever one month after SARS-CoV-2 infection, diagnosed with new-onset ulcerative colitis.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae tested negative via stool cultures and gastrointestinal multiplex PCR panel

evidence_items.source_quote: Stool studies, including cultures for common pathogens, parasites, tests for Clostridium difficile GDH, toxins A and B all returned negative. Moreover, the gastrointestinal PCR panel test for common pathogens was also negative.
evidence_items.test_name: Stool culture and gastrointestinal PCR panel

evidence_items.source_quote: This panel test targets bacterial infections (Campylobacter jejuni, Campylobacter coli, C. difficile toxin A/B, Salmonella spp, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, Enteroaggregative E. coli, Enteropathogenic E. coli, Enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shigella-like toxin-producing E. coli, Shigella spp), parasitic infections (Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia) and viral infections (Adenovirus, Astrovirus, Norovirus, Rotavirus A, Sapovirus).

step10_contradiction_notes: Stool cultures and gastrointestinal PCR panel targeting Vibrio cholerae were negative; colonoscopy and biopsy confirmed ulcerative colitis.
rationale: A 74-year-old male developed fever and bloody diarrhea one month after COVID-19. Stool cultures and a gastrointestinal PCR panel targeting Vibrio cholerae and other enteric pathogens were all negative, and ileocolonoscopy with biopsy established new-onset ulcerative colitis -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 21-year-old Mexican male in China with Vi-negative Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi typhoid fever complicated by acute acalculous cholecystitis and massive intestinal hemorrhage.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 tested negative by both rapid test and fecal bacterial isolation

evidence_items.source_quote: Rapid tests for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 were also negative.
evidence_items.test_name: Rapid test for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139

evidence_items.source_quote: The following test results were negative: the full panel for hepatitis; serologic tests for hantavirus, EB virus, and TORCH (Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and other pathogenic microorganisms); nucleic acid assay for cytomegalovirus, EB virus, and the new Bunya virus; fecal bacterial isolation of V. cholerae O1/O139 and Escherichia coli O157:H7.

step10_contradiction_notes: Both rapid tests and fecal bacterial isolation for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 were negative; blood culture confirmed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
rationale: A 21-year-old male presented with fever, watery diarrhea, jaundice, acute acalculous cholecystitis, and massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Rapid testing for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 at the initial hospital and fecal bacterial isolation of V. cholerae O1/O139 at the referral hospital were both explicitly negative, while blood cultures confirmed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 10-year-old boy admitted to PICU with severe Cryptosporidium parvum diarrhea, hypovolemic shock, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and pancreatitis.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio cholerae slide agglutination test explicitly negative

evidence_items.source_quote: Furthermore, PCR results of Entamoeba trophozoites and cysts, Enterovirus 71, Coxsackie virus A16, and Vibrio cholerae slide agglutination test were all negative.

step10_contradiction_notes: Vibrio cholerae slide agglutination test was negative, and blood/anal-swab mNGS confirmed Cryptosporidium parvum.
rationale: A 10-year-old immunocompetent boy presented to the PICU with severe watery diarrhea, shock, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and pancreatitis. A Vibrio cholerae slide agglutination test was explicitly negative, and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of blood and anal swabs confirmed Cryptosporidium parvum infection -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 38-year-old female with PU.1-mutated agammaglobulinemia, chronic enteropathy, recurrent infections, and fatal rapidly progressive neurocognitive disorder.

step4_condition_matched: Vibrio (V. parahaemolyticus/V. vulnificus/V. cholerae) and Vibrio cholerae tested on gastrointestinal multiplex PCR panel, which detected only Clostridioides difficile (toxin A/B) alongside Norovirus GI/GII

evidence_items.source_quote: A gastrointestinal multiplex PCR panel (Campylobacter (C. jejuni/C. coli/C. upsaliensis), Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile (toxin A/B), Plesiomonas shigelloides, Salmonella, Yersinia enterocolitica, Vibrio (V. parahaemolyticus/V. vulnificus/V. cholerae), Vibrio cholerae, Enteroaggregative E. coli, Enteropathogenic E. coli, Enterotoxigenic E. coli lt/st, Shiga-like toxin-producing E. coli stx1/stx2, E. coli O157, Shigella/Enteroinvasive E. coli; Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia; Adenovirus F40/41, Astrovirus, Norovirus GI/GII, Rotavirus A, Sapovirus (I, II, IV, and V) also revealed Clostridium difficile (toxin A/B), and the patient was treated with oral vancomycin at a daily dose of 500 mg for 14 days.

step10_contradiction_notes: Gastrointestinal multiplex PCR panel covering Vibrio cholerae detected only Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B (in addition to Norovirus GI/GII RNA).
rationale: A 38-year-old female with PU.1-mutated agammaglobulinemia underwent stool microbiological testing during a severe diarrheal episode prior to her neurocognitive decline. Stool testing identified Norovirus GI/GII RNA, and a 22-target gastrointestinal multiplex PCR panel (explicitly including Vibrio and Vibrio cholerae) detected only Clostridioides difficile (toxin A/B), ruling out cholera -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 60-year-old female presenting with acute watery gastroenteritis and shock, diagnosed with ceftriaxone-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Newport.

step4_condition_matched: Empirical IV doxycycline initiated to cover suspected Vibrio cholerae, then discontinued after stool culture and NICED reference speciation confirmed oxidase-negative Salmonella enterica serovar Newport

evidence_items.source_quote: In view of the shock caused by gastroenteritis, the patient was empirically started on piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g QID to empirically cover Gram-negative infections, doxycycline (injection) 100 mg BD to cover Vibrio cholerae, and metronidazole (injection) 500 mg TID to cover protozoans.

Consequently, the isolate was forwarded to the National Institute of Cholera and Enteric Diseases (NICED) in Kolkata, West Bengal, India, for speciation and serotyping. The NICED report identified the isolate as Salmonella enterica serovar Newport with resistance to ceftriaxone.
evidence_items.test_name: Stool culture and reference serotyping at NICED

evidence_items.source_quote: Once gastroenteritis due to NTS with ceftriaxone resistance was diagnosed, the injection of piperacillin-tazobactam was continued for 9 days, and doxycycline and metronidazole were stopped.

step10_contradiction_notes: Initial empirical coverage with IV doxycycline for suspected Vibrio cholerae was discontinued once stool culture grew cytochrome-oxidase-negative bacilli identified by the National Institute of Cholera and Enteric Diseases (NICED) as Salmonella enterica serovar Newport.
rationale: A 60-year-old woman presented with acute watery diarrhea, vomiting, and shock and received empirical intravenous doxycycline to cover Vibrio cholerae alongside piperacillin-tazobactam and metronidazole. Stool culture isolated cytochrome-oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli confirmed by the National Institute of Cholera and Enteric Diseases (NICED) as ceftriaxone-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Newport, leading to discontinuation of doxycycline -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 14-year-old female returning to Moscow from the Maldives with imported dengue fever and respiratory Mycoplasma pneumoniae co-infection.

step4_condition_matched: Differential diagnostic examination for cholera performed and excluded in a patient with confirmed dengue fever and Mycoplasma pneumoniae co-infection

evidence_items.source_quote: For differential diagnostics, examination for malaria and cholera, acute intestinal infections, herpes virus infections, and examination of oropharyngeal swab materials for nucleic acids of 16 respiratory pathogens were performed.

Thus, based on the data of the disease history, epidemiological anamnesis, complaints, physical and laboratory-instrumental examination data, the final diagnosis was established. The primary diagnosis: dengue fever of moderate severity. The secondary diagnosis: mycoplasma infection (M. pneumoniae) of moderate severity.
evidence_items.target_concept: Dengue fever and Mycoplasma pneumoniae co-infection (cholera excluded)

step10_contradiction_notes: Differential diagnostic testing for malaria, cholera, and acute intestinal infections excluded cholera; dengue virus RNA NAAT and M. pneumoniae IgM confirmed the final co-infection diagnosis.
rationale: A 14-year-old girl returning to Moscow from the Maldives presented with fever, rash, epistaxis, cough, abdominal pain, and liquid stools. Differential diagnostic testing for malaria, cholera, and acute intestinal infections was performed, and the final confirmed diagnoses were moderate dengue fever (positive blood dengue antigen RDT and arbovirus RNA NAAT) and Mycoplasma pneumoniae respiratory co-infection (positive M. pneumoniae IgM), ruling out cholera -> NEGATIVE.
